Let's start with a decimal point. In 2006, Arizona voters considered Proposition 203,
which was supposed to fund early childhood programs by increasing the cigarette tax.
The backers meant to raise the tax by 80 cents per pack. But the ballot's explanation of
what a yes vote would do described it as an increase of 0.80 cents per pack. And those
aren't the same thing. If you write 80 cents, you mean 80 pennies. You can also write that
amount with a dollar sign as $0.8, but 0.8 cents means 8 tenths of one cent, so the
ballot's version was actually a hundred times smaller than the intended tax. The word decimal
itself is all about ten. It comes from the Latin de chimus, meaning tenth, and the phrase
decimal point has been used in English since at least 1711. In the Arizona summary, that
tiny decimal point before the 80 made a huge difference. In fact, the Arizona Republic

40 public meetings. Finally, a sharp-eyed newspaper reader noticed the problem, but unfortunately
after early voting had started. Fortunately, though, the full text of the initiative was

cents for a standard pack of 20. After voters approved the measure, Arizona's Attorney

was written correctly. It was just the summary that was wrong.

would raise certain income tax rates by quote, 3.46% and by 4.46%.

If you were talking percentages, the taxes would have gone up approximately 76% and 98%.
A percentage increase tells you the size of a change relative to the original number.
